transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman, President Trump says major tech companies
have agreed to come together and self-police their artificial intelligence products.
The voluntary agreement comes after about 30 executives from the biggest U.S. tech companies
gathered at the White House.
NPR's Emily Feng has more.
Asked whether this agreement was legally enforceable, Trump replied.
I think it's morally binding, yeah.
He argued that private tech companies can be trusted to regulate themselves.
The accord asks companies to monitor their A.I. products and set up internal controls
to make sure they do not hack into other systems.
Their companies are at stake.
If something goes wrong, their companies are at stake, they're not going to let that happen.
This is going to be all for the good and we're going to have it be nice and safe, and they're
really going to be policing each other.
Those involved offered no details on how that would work.
Emily Feng, NPR News, the White House.
The U.S. Supreme Court will let the Trump administration deport migrants to countries
that they don't have any links to.
This is an interim opinion until the High Court can hear the case in full in December.
The Trump administration has been deporting migrants to places such as Somalia and South
Sudan, countries where there is conflict.
NPR's Linda Kenyon reports opponents say the policy permanently harms migrants.
The National Immigration Litigation Alliance, which is representing the migrants facing
deportation, says that these immigrants have, quote, "faced prolonged and arbitrary detention,
beatings and sexual assault and disappearance."
And they also say that there is the possibility that they would be sent back to their home
countries where they would face persecution.
NPR's Linda Kenyon reporting.
The Pentagon says the U.S. military has formally left Iraq.
In a statement, the Defense Department says the U.S. has concluded its military mission
there.
The U.S. says Iraq now has the primary responsibility for addressing its own military challenges.
NPR has learned of a plan for a massive new data center on federal land in Utah.
As NPR's Jeff Brumfield reports, it would involve building hundreds of nuclear reactors.
The proposal seen by NPR came from the company Valor Automics.
Valor already has a test reactor operating in Utah, but it wants to build around 450 more
small nuclear reactors on 9,000 acres of federal land.
The reactors would provide power for data centers, among other things.
Neil Clark with the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance says Valor isn't the only company
quietly seeking to build data centers on public lands.
It's pretty obvious that they're trying to keep these proposals and these processes totally
under the radar to make sure the public is kept in the dark.
The Bureau of Land Management says the public will have an opportunity to comment on the
proposal after the agency reviews the application for completeness.
Jeff Brumfield, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR.
Forecasters say Hurricane Polo has broken up over northern Mexico, but its heavy moisture
is still streaming north into the U.S.
There are flood watches and warnings posted from the desert southwest up to Illinois.
There are flash flood warnings in parts of New Mexico and Texas.
A Northern California police department has been released from what's thought to be the
longest period of federal law enforcement oversight ever.
From member station KQED, Katie D. Benedetti has more.
The Oakland Police Department has been under watch for more than 20 years, following a
major police brutality and corruption scandal involving a group of officers known as the
riders.
Now, a federal judge says the department has come into substantial compliance with more
than 50 court-mandated reforms related to use of force, misconduct investigations and
other operations.
Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee called the decision historic.
This is a new police department.
The work that has taken place over several mayors, over several police chiefs, that work
has led us to this day.
City officials say the department is focused on continuing to rebuild community trust.
For NPR News, I'm Katie D. Benedetti in San Francisco.
There's a winner in the Fat Bear Week contest.
It's the Brown Bear Backpack.
He's estimated to weigh more than 1,000 pounds.
The contest is held by Katmai National Park and Preserve in Alaska.
Park Rangers say that a record number of voters worldwide cast online ballots.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: President Trump says major tech companies agreed to self-police artificial intelligence products
Supreme Court allows Trump administration to deport migrants to countries without links
Pentagon says U.S. military has formally concluded its mission and left Iraq
Company Valor Automics proposes 450 small nuclear reactors on federal land in Utah
Hurricane Polo breaks up over northern Mexico, heavy moisture streams north into U.S.
Oakland Police Department released from over 20 years of federal law enforcement oversight
Brown Bear Backpack wins Fat Bear Week contest at Katmai National Park, Alaska
